analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above $50 million, with a higher rate on billionaires.
analysis.headline: A bill to tax household wealth above $50 million — 2% above that level and an added 3% on fortunes over $1 billion — has 11 Senate supporters and has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing since its introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates an annual tax on the net worth of the wealthiest households: 2% on assets above $50 million, plus an extra 3% on everything above $1 billion. It would also pour money into IRS enforcement, require banks and businesses to report asset values, and automatically double the billionaire surcharge if Congress ever passes a universal government health program. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the direct benefit would be the public purse: the tax is designed to raise substantial revenue from roughly the wealthiest one-tenth of one percent of households, and the bill authorizes $100 billion over a decade for IRS enforcement, taxpayer services, and systems modernization. All households with net worth under $50 million — more than 99.9% of Americans — would owe nothing. The bill contains no spending programs itself, so any benefit to ordinary people depends on what Congress later does with the revenue; the one hardwired benefit is that the billionaire rate doubles to fund universal health coverage if such a program is enacted.

how_it_helps.text: Places the tax burden entirely on households with net worth above $50 million; the 2% rate applies only to the portion of wealth above $50 million and nothing applies below that threshold.

Adds a 3% surcharge on wealth above $1 billion, rising to 6% if Congress establishes a universal health insurance program that bars duplicate private coverage — directly tying billionaire wealth to funding health care for everyone else.
Authorizes $100 billion in appropriations for fiscal years 2027–2037: $70 billion for IRS enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for business systems modernization.

Cracks down on avoidance: it targets assets hidden in foreign entities, leverages foreign-account reporting data, closes trusts used to shield family wealth, and requires an annual audit of at least 30% of taxpayers who owe the tax.
Gives taxpayers with illiquid assets — such as owners of businesses they cannot sell quickly — up to five years to pay, and excludes household items under $50,000.

analysis.who_pays: Households and multibeneficiary trusts with net worth over $50 million would pay the tax annually on the net value of nearly all their assets worldwide — including private business interests, stock, and property — with no ability to deduct the tax from their income taxes. Wealthy owners of private companies bear the sharpest risk: the bill directs the Treasury Secretary to set valuation rules for hard-to-price assets, including formulaic methods and back-charging based on eventual sale prices, and it layers penalties of 30–50% on valuations that come in far below what the IRS determines is correct. Financial institutions and business entities would take on new reporting duties, including estimating the value of the businesses themselves. Anyone renouncing US citizenship to escape the tax would owe 40% on their wealth at expatriation.

drawbacks.text: Valuing private companies, art, and other illiquid assets is inherently imprecise. The bill responds by letting the IRS use formulaic and retrospective valuation methods and by imposing a 30–50% penalty on taxpayers whose declared values fall far below the government's estimate — a system that could mean large tax bills on assets the owner has not sold and cannot easily price.

The tax would fall on wealth, not income, so a family with a valuable business but little cash could owe the tax every year even in unprofitable ones. The bill offers up to five years' deferral, but deferral is discretionary and interest and liability accumulate.

It gives the Treasury Secretary broad authority to force financial institutions and business entities to report asset values and to estimate the worth of businesses themselves — a significant compliance burden that would be borne by banks and companies, and could be passed along or used to lobby against the tax.

The bill specifies no use for the revenue other than IRS administration and a conditional link to universal health coverage, so any concrete benefit to ordinary taxpayers — a lower deficit, funded programs, or tax cuts for working families — depends entirely on separate legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is large and concentrated on a tiny group: an annual tax on roughly the wealthiest one-tenth of one percent of households, with aggressive anti-avoidance and audit provisions that make it more enforceable than most tax bills. The costs are real but narrower: administrative complexity and valuation disputes for the ultrawealthy and their businesses, new reporting burdens for financial institutions, and the difficulty of paying a wealth tax out of illiquid assets. The bill's honest weakness is not its design but its reach — with only 11 Senate supporters, it reflects no realistic path to law in this Congress, and because it specifies no spending, its practical benefit to ordinary people remains theoretical.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren and 10 Democratic colleagues introduced the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2026 in the Senate on March 26, 2026.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where tax legislation is considered.

No further action appears in the record: the committee has not held a hearing or markup, the bill has not come to the floor, and no companion action in the House is recorded. With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and the bill's sponsors numbering 11 Democrats, it lacks the support to clear either a committee or the 60-vote threshold generally needed to advance most legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with net worth above $50 million and their businesses are better off so far, because the tax has not advanced; they keep their wealth untaxed. Supporters of the bill are no worse off financially, but the bill's 11 sponsors can point only to a referral, not progress.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and assembled 10 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 10 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors: Duckworth, Hirono, Markey, Merkley, Schiff, Smith, Schatz, Van Hollen, Welch, and Whitehouse.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — after it was referred on the day of introduction.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsors or cosponsors the bill, leaving it far short of the support needed to reach the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors are Democrats; no Republican and no independent has signed on, in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 seats.

industries.note: The bill's direct payers: an annual tax of 2% on net worth above $50 million and an extra 3% above $1 billion, with audits of at least 30% of them each year. Their interest in stopping it runs against the public interest in whoever ultimately funds the revenue.

industries.industry: Privately held businesses and their ultra-wealthy owners
industries.note: Owners of companies without a market price face IRS formulaic valuations and penalties of 30–50% for large understatement, plus taxes on value they have never realized by selling.

The bill makes them the reporting backbone for asset values and foreign-account enforcement, adding compliance costs; the same reporting helps catch evasion that ordinary taxpayers otherwise subsidize.

industries.industry: Wealth management, tax advisory, and estate planning
industries.note: A new wealth tax would create a vast compliance market for these firms, even as the bill's anti-avoidance, trust-attribution, and expatriation rules shrink the avoidance schemes they currently sell.

industries.industry: Art, collectibles, and luxury asset markets
industries.note: Collectibles, boats, aircraft, and appreciating antiques are explicitly brought into the tax base, so these markets lose their current treatment as untracked wealth.
The bill authorizes $100 billion over eleven years for enforcement, taxpayer services, and modernization — capacity that also improves service and collection for ordinary filers.

analysis.trajectory: The realistic path is no path: with 11 supporters in a 55-seat Republican Senate and no recorded committee action since referral, the bill is very likely to sit in the Finance Committee until this Congress ends in early January 2027 and die without a vote, as prior versions of this proposal did. At most, it functions as a position statement for a future Democratic Congress.
